## Overview

`tripletTools` ships several independent HTCondor workflows for offloading expensive, embarrassingly-parallel computations — grid searches, permutation tests, per-participant fits, joint manifold estimation — to a cluster (e.g. UW–Madison's CHTC) instead of running them serially (or even multicore) on your own machine. This vignette covers four of them in depth; a fifth (the choice-model recovery sweep) has its own `README_recovery_sweep.md` in `inst/condor/` rather than a section here yet.

All four covered here share the same design: a small, dependency-light **Python** script (the *orchestrator*) runs on the submit node and does the actual `condor_submit`/`condor_wait` work — **no R installation is needed on the submit node**, only Python 3 and PyYAML. Every real computation (each embedding fit, each comparison) instead runs *inside the `tripletTools` container image* via HTCondor's `container` universe, dispatched as a per-job R script. This split matters because CHTC's execute nodes are heterogeneous and ephemeral — you cannot assume any of them has R, `tripletTools`, or the `triplet-embeddings` conda environment pre-installed, so every job carries its own environment with it via the container instead. (Workflow 4's first version broke this rule for one cheap, non-parallel step — see its own section below for why that was a real problem on a real submit node, and how it was fixed.)

| Workflow | What it does | Local R equivalent | Files (all in `inst/condor/`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dimensionality search → learning curve → final fit | Picks an embedding dimension, sanity-checks it against a learning curve, and produces a production embedding | `estimate_dimensionality()` / `estimate_learning_curve()` | `condor_workflow.py`, `condor_fit.R`, `params_template.yml` |
| Group-difference permutation test | Tests whether two participant groups' embeddings differ reliably, via a size-matched permutation null | `group_difference_test()` | `condor_group_diff_workflow.py`, `condor_group_fit.R`, `condor_group_compare.R`, `group_diff_params_template.yml` |
| Per-participant individual embeddings | Fits a separate embedding for every participant, concatenated into one CSV | `run_embeddings_from_list()` (its "individual" output) | `condor_individual_embeddings_workflow.py`, `condor_individual_fit.R`, `individual_embeddings_params_template.yml` |
| Joint geometry+choice-model manifold estimation | Jointly estimates, per participant, a 1-D manifold position determining both a real re-fit embedding and a choice-model shape alpha | (no local equivalent — the fully rigorous version requires Condor-scale parallel embedding refits) | `condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py`, `condor_joint_manifold_fit.R`, `condor_joint_manifold_update.R`, `joint_manifold_params_template.yml` |

Each workflow also has its own quick-reference `README_*.md` alongside its scripts in `inst/condor/` — this vignette covers the same ground in more depth and in one place, but the READMEs are there for exactly the moment you've sparse-cloned just `inst/condor/` (see below) and want the deployment steps without leaving that directory.

---

## Prerequisites (submit node only)

- Python 3
- PyYAML: `pip install --user pyyaml`
- HTCondor client tools (`condor_submit`, `condor_wait`, `condor_q`, `condor_ssh_to_job`) — already present on any CHTC access point

None of the three workflows need R, conda, or `tripletTools` itself installed on the submit node. Those are only ever needed inside the container image that each job runs in.

---

## Getting the workflow files: a sparse clone per analysis

The only part of the repository these workflows need is `inst/condor/` — everything else (the vendored Python embedding backend, R source, vignettes, bundled example datasets) is irrelevant on the submit node. At the same time, it's worth getting a fresh copy **per analysis** rather than repeatedly reusing one long-lived shared clone: some of these workflows span hours to days (e.g. a fit stage followed hours later by a compare stage), and a `git pull` to the shared clone in between could silently change the code partway through a single run. A bare copied file, on its own, also carries no record of which commit produced it.

Combining both concerns — avoid pulling the whole repo, but still get a verifiable, frozen snapshot — git's `--filter=blob:none` partial clone plus `sparse-checkout` does exactly this:

```{r sparse-clone, engine = "bash"}
git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout --depth 1 \
  https://github.com/Knowledge-and-Concepts-Lab/tripletTools.git my_analysis
cd my_analysis
git sparse-checkout init --cone
git sparse-checkout set inst/condor
git checkout main
cd inst/condor
```

`--filter=blob:none` means the server only sends file *contents* for what you actually check out, not the whole repository's history of blobs; `sparse-checkout` then limits the working tree to just `inst/condor/`. The result is a directory containing only the condor workflow files — nothing unrelated in sight — while still being a real git repository, so `git log -1` inside `my_analysis` gives you a genuine, verifiable record of exactly which commit produced the scripts you ran.

Two things worth knowing:

- `inst/condor/` is still one directory level below the clone root (`my_analysis/inst/condor/`, not `my_analysis/`) — a fixed consequence of these files living inside an R package's `inst/` directory in the source repo. In practice you just `cd` into it once and treat it as your working directory from then on (uploading data there, editing configs there, running the orchestrator there).
- Cone-mode sparse-checkout needs git ≥ 2.25. If that's ever unavailable, fall back to a plain shallow clone (`git clone --depth 1 ... my_analysis`) and `cd my_analysis/inst/condor` — more bytes on disk, but identical otherwise, including the commit-hash provenance.

---

## General deployment procedure

Every workflow follows the same shape, once you're sitting in your cloned `inst/condor/`:

1. **Prepare your input data file(s).** At minimum, a combined triplet-judgment CSV — one row per triplet trial, with a `worker_id` column and the format `get.combined()` reads (see `inst/extdata/icon_all_triplets.csv` for an example). This is your raw data exactly as collected; nothing needs to be precomputed. The group-difference workflow additionally needs a group-labels CSV (see its section below). Upload data files into the same directory as the scripts (`scp`, or however you already move data onto the access point).

2. **Copy the relevant `*_params_template.yml` and edit it.** Every field is documented with inline comments in the template itself; at minimum you'll set `output_dir` and (for the two embedding-fitting workflows) `d`, chosen beforehand via a local `estimate_dimensionality()` run — never re-selected mid-workflow, since doing so per replicate/participant would be prohibitively slow and would entangle dimensionality selection with whatever the workflow is actually testing.

   ```{r copy-config, engine = "bash"}
   cp params_template.yml my_params.yml   # or group_diff_params_template.yml / individual_embeddings_params_template.yml
   ```

3. **Run the driver script.** Since it only *orchestrates* — every actual embedding fit or comparison runs as its own Condor job, not in this process — it's safe to run directly on the access point inside a persistent session (`screen`/`tmux`/`nohup`) rather than as a Condor job itself:

   ```{r run-driver, engine = "bash"}
   python3 condor_workflow.py triplet_data.csv my_params.yml
   ```

4. **Collect outputs from `output_dir`** (set in your edited config) once the driver prints its final summary and exits. Each workflow's section below details exactly what lands there.

---

## The container image

Every job — regardless of which workflow submitted it — runs inside the same `tripletTools` container image via `universe = container`, built from:

```
Dockerfile                                # builds the runtime image
.github/workflows/docker-publish.yml      # builds + publishes it to ghcr.io on push
```

The image layers a base R install, Miniconda, the `triplet-embeddings` conda environment (built via this package's own `setup_python_env()`, so it's created exactly the way a local install would be), and `tripletTools` itself. GitHub Actions rebuilds and pushes it to `ghcr.io/<org>/<repo>` automatically whenever `Dockerfile`, `R/`, `inst/python/`, `inst/requirements.txt`, `DESCRIPTION`, or the workflow file itself change on `main` — pure documentation or `inst/condor/`-only changes do **not** trigger a rebuild. Every build publishes two tags: a floating `:latest` and an immutable `:sha-<full 40-character commit SHA>`.

**Pin to a specific SHA tag if you need certainty about which code ran.** `:latest` moves with every rebuild; a job submitted mid-run under `:latest` and a job submitted an hour later after someone else pushed a change could silently run different code. The immutable `:sha-...` tag never changes once published, so pinning to it in your config gives the same kind of provenance guarantee as the sparse-clone commit hash above:

```yaml
condor:
  container_image: docker://ghcr.io/knowledge-and-concepts-lab/triplettools:sha-<full-commit-sha>
```

**Apptainer/HTCondor caches the pulled image per execute node**, which is fine at the job counts these workflows generate (dozens to a few thousand per run). If you're deploying often enough that repeated `docker://` pulls become a bottleneck, build the image into a `.sif` once and stage it instead of pulling from the registry every time — point `condor.container_image` in your config at CHTC's OSDF/Pelican staging path convention instead of the `docker://` reference:

```yaml
condor:
  container_image: osdf:///chtc$ENV(STAGING)/containers/tripletTools_v1.sif
```

(this also needs `requirements = (Target.HasCHTCStaging == true)` added to the relevant submit file in whichever workflow's `.py` you're running, if you go this route). Give the `.sif` a version suffix and update the config's path when you rebuild it, rather than overwriting the old filename — OSDF/Pelican caches by path, so reusing a filename can serve stale content.

**Disk requests are sized for the container.** Pulling and unpacking it (R + conda + PyTorch) adds several GB on top of whatever a job itself transfers, so every shipped `*_params_template.yml` defaults `condor.resources.request_disk` to `8GB`. Override it in your copy of the config if you need more.

**CHTC staging paths**, if your triplet dataset itself is large enough to need `/staging` rather than ordinary `transfer_input_files` (CHTC's general guidance: under 1GB per file stays in `/home`; 1–30GB goes to personal staging): personal staging areas are at `/staging/<first letter of your netid>/<netid>`, exposed as `$STAGING` on access points and `$ENV(STAGING)` in submit files. A job that reads staging directly needs `requirements = (Target.HasCHTCStaging == true)`.

---

## Troubleshooting a job that seems stuck

All three workflows submit jobs the same way, so the same diagnostic steps apply regardless of which one you're running.

**Check its status first.**

```{r check-status, engine = "bash"}
condor_q <cluster>.<proc>
```

`JobStatus = 2` means genuinely running; `5` means held (check `condor_q -better-analyze <jobid>` for why); a job can also be legitimately **suspended** (not killed, not held) on a shared/opportunistic execute slot under CPU contention — check for this with:

```{r check-suspension, engine = "bash"}
condor_q -long <jobid> | grep -E "JobStatus|TotalSuspensions|LastSuspensionTime"
```

A suspended job's CPU time genuinely stops accruing while paused, then resumes on its own — nothing is wrong, it's just waiting its turn.

**A polling-lag caveat before you conclude anything from `RemoteUserCpu`.** `condor_q`'s numbers come from periodic updates the execute node pushes back to the schedd (commonly every several minutes), not a live feed. If you check `RemoteUserCpu` twice only a minute or two apart and see no change, that may just mean it hasn't refreshed yet — not that the job is stalled. Re-check with a longer gap before drawing conclusions.

**You cannot tail a running job's `.out`/`.err` for live progress.** Every submit file here uses `when_to_transfer_output = ON_EXIT`, so those files only transfer back to the submit node once the job actually finishes. A quiet local `.out` file means you can't see it yet, not that the job is quiet.

**The definitive check, if your pool has it enabled:**

```{r ssh-to-job, engine = "bash"}
condor_ssh_to_job <jobid>
```

This drops you directly into the job's own running sandbox on the execute node (ignore any `groups: cannot find name for group ID ...` warnings on login — harmless noise from resolving container UID/GID mappings). From there:

```{r inspect-process, engine = "bash"}
ps aux              # find the R process; check %CPU and STAT
cat /proc/<pid>/status | grep State
free -h             # memory/swap pressure
df -h .             # disk full in the sandbox?
```

`STAT` of `R`/`S` with nonzero, climbing `%CPU` means it's genuinely computing — a job can legitimately take much longer than its siblings (e.g. `max_epochs`/`tol_window` haven't triggered early stopping yet, or it landed on the larger side of an unequal group split) without anything being wrong. `D` (uninterruptible sleep, usually I/O-blocked) or a missing/zombied process is a real problem. Exiting this session (`exit` or Ctrl+D) only closes the debug shell — it does not touch the job's own process tree.

**If it really is stuck:** `condor_vacate_job <jobid>` is the right first move — it evicts the job and lets HTCondor re-match and restart it fresh, keeping the *same* job ID, so the orchestrator's `condor_wait` (which is watching for that specific ID) needs no changes and keeps working correctly. Only fall back to `condor_rm` + manually resubmitting that one job (capturing its `Arguments`/`TransferInput` from `condor_q -long` first, since you'll need them to rebuild a one-off submit file) if the same job stalls again after vacating — that points to something specific to its data or arguments rather than an unlucky execute node, and a full remove is a more invasive fix worth reserving for that case.

---

## A job finishes cleanly but its output file is empty

This is a different failure mode from a stuck job above — the job is no longer running at all, `condor_q`/`condor_history` shows `Normal termination (return value 0)`, its `.err` is empty, and yet its expected output CSV is either missing or exists with 0 bytes.

A clean exit code and an empty `.err` are the important clues: `Rscript` exits with status 1 by default on any uncaught R error, so a genuinely clean exit means the per-job R script ran to completion without error — it's not a data problem or a bug in the comparison/fit logic. This is consistent with a file-transfer issue instead: when on the order of a hundred jobs finish within the same narrow window, each trying to transfer its (tiny) output file back to the submit node at nearly the same moment, some of those transfers can silently come back empty. This was first hit running the group-difference workflow at 627 participants / 100 permutations, where roughly half of 101 comparison jobs came back empty despite every one logging a clean exit.

**All three workflows now handle this automatically.** Every job-submission stage verifies each expected output file after `condor_wait` returns, and resubmits just the ones that came back missing or empty — up to 5 additional attempts — before failing with a clear error naming exactly which jobs never produced valid output (rather than the unhelpful bare traceback this used to produce). You'll see this in the driver's own output as e.g.:

```
[condor_group_diff] Stage 2 (comparisons): 53 of 101 output(s) missing/empty after attempt 1 -- retrying (...)
[condor_group_diff] Stage 2 (comparisons): 4 of 53 output(s) missing/empty after attempt 2 -- retrying (...)
```

Nothing further to do in that case — just let it keep running.

**If you want to reduce how often this happens in the first place** (rather than just cleaning up after it), set `condor.batch_size` in your config to cap how many jobs run/finish concurrently:

```yaml
condor:
  batch_size: 25
```

This submits jobs in sequential chunks of that size instead of all at once, directly limiting how many can ever finish in the same narrow window. It costs some wall-clock time if the pool has free slots to spare (batches run one after another, not all in parallel), so it's a tradeoff worth making only if the automatic retries above are firing often enough to be a real nuisance.

**If a comparison-only stage exhausts its retries anyway,** and the underlying fits are already done, it's often faster to finish that one stage locally than to keep fighting the transfer path: the group-difference workflow's Stage 2 in particular is cheap (reading two small embedding CSVs and one Procrustes alignment per replicate), so pulling `stage1_fit/` down to wherever you have `tripletTools` installed and computing the correlations directly avoids Condor's compare stage entirely for that run:

```r
library(tripletTools)

stage1_dir <- "stage1_fit"   # after rsync-ing it down from the submit node

read_embedding <- function(path) {
  df <- read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  m <- as.matrix(df[, grepl("^dim_", names(df)), drop = FALSE])
  rownames(m) <- df$item
  m
}

side_a_files <- list.files(stage1_dir, pattern = "^embedding_rep(\\d+)_sideA\\.csv$")
replicate_ids <- sort(as.integer(sub("^embedding_rep(\\d+)_sideA\\.csv$", "\\1", side_a_files)))

results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(replicate_ids, function(rep_id) {
  emb_a <- read_embedding(file.path(stage1_dir, sprintf("embedding_rep%d_sideA.csv", rep_id)))
  emb_b <- read_embedding(file.path(stage1_dir, sprintf("embedding_rep%d_sideB.csv", rep_id)))
  emb_b <- emb_b[rownames(emb_a), , drop = FALSE]
  sdist <- get.rep.dist(list(a = emb_a, b = emb_b))
  data.frame(replicate_id = rep_id, is_true = (rep_id == 0), correlation = 1 - sdist[1, 2])
}))

observed    <- results$correlation[results$is_true]
null_values <- results$correlation[!results$is_true]
p_value     <- (1 + sum(null_values <= observed)) / (1 + length(null_values))
```

---

## A job goes held mid-run

`JobStatus = 5` (held, from the status-check above) used to mean the whole run would simply stall — `condor_wait` only returns once every job in its log has either terminated or been removed, and a held job does neither until a human releases or removes it. This happened for real on an overnight joint-manifold deployment: one job held with `invalid mount config for type "bind": bind source path does not exist: /cvmfs` — a broken Docker/CVMFS mount specific to one bad execute node, unrelated to the job's own code or data — and the run sat there until morning.

**All five workflows now handle this automatically.** `submit_and_wait()` polls with `condor_wait -wait <seconds>` in a loop instead of blocking on one open-ended call, and after each timeout checks `condor_q -held` for that submission's cluster and auto-releases anything it finds — up to 3 releases per job before giving up. A transient bad-execute-node problem like the `/cvmfs` one above almost always succeeds on the very next release, since the matchmaker reassigns a released job to a different slot rather than retrying the same one. You'll see this in the driver's own output as e.g.:

```
[condor_joint_manifold] embedding refits: job 7202726.21 is held (auto-release 1/3) -- Error from slot1_11@e2472.chtc.wisc.edu: Error response from daemon: invalid mount config for type "bind": bind source path does not exist: /cvmfs
```

Nothing further to do in that case — just let it keep running. If a job holds for the *same* reason three times in a row, the driver gives up with a clear error naming the job and the hold reason, since at that point it's more likely a real, persistent problem (e.g. a genuinely bad `request_memory`/`request_disk`, or a bad container tag) than bad luck with execute nodes, and worth looking at directly (`condor_q -held`, `condor_q -better-analyze <jobid>`) before releasing it again by hand.

---

## Workflow 1: Dimensionality search, learning curve, and final embedding fit

For the common case of "pick a dimension, check it against a learning curve, and fit the best embedding," `condor_workflow.py` runs all three stages back to back, dispatching every individual fit to HTCondor as its own job.

```{r condor-run-workflow, engine = "bash"}
python3 condor_workflow.py triplet_data.csv my_params.yml
```

This produces, in `output_dir`:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `dimensionality_results.csv` / `dimensionality_summary.csv` | `estimate_dimensionality()`'s `results`/`summary`, one Condor job per (dimension, restart) |
| `learning_curve_results.csv` / `learning_curve_summary.csv` | `estimate_learning_curve()`'s `results`/`summary`, at the `best_d` selected above, one Condor job per (fraction, restart) |
| `best_embedding.csv` | The final embedding, fit at `best_d` on the *full* dataset (item names in the `item` column) |
| `best_embedding_history.csv` | That final fit's per-epoch training history (loss, accuracy, `norm_ratio`, ...) |
| `run_manifest.txt` | Package version, input paths, `best_d`, and final loss, for provenance |

`seed`, `geometry`, `radius`, and `norm_penalty` apply to all three stages, so they describe one coherent embedding space throughout; `max_epochs`/`tolerance`/`tol_window`/`device`/`internal_test_frac`/Condor `resources` can be overridden per stage — see the comments in `params_template.yml`. See `vignette("embedding_vignette")` for the full statistical rationale behind `internal_test_frac` and why the final embedding is a dedicated fit rather than a reused learning-curve restart.

### Recomputing a summary yourself, without refitting anything

`condor_workflow.py` already writes the `_summary.csv` files above as part of a normal run, so you don't usually need to do this. Two situations where you do: the workflow's own aggregation step didn't complete (the same output-transfer failure described in ["A job finishes cleanly but its output file is empty"](#a-job-finishes-cleanly-but-its-output-file-is-empty) above can in principle hit *any* stage's many-small-jobs pattern, including the local aggregation reading them back), or you want to try a different `best_d_norm_penalty` after the fact without re-fitting a single embedding. `summarize_dimensionality()` and `summarize_learning_curve()` are exactly the aggregation logic `estimate_dimensionality()`/`estimate_learning_curve()` use internally (see their own `$summary` return element), exported so you can apply the identical logic directly to a `dimensionality_results.csv`/`learning_curve_results.csv` you already have on disk — or, as below, any data frame in that same shape, however you collected it.

`dimensionality_results.csv` is just the row-bound output of every `condor_fit.R --stage=dimensionality` job in that stage: one row per `(d, restart)` with columns `d`, `restart`, `loss`, `accuracy`, `epoch`, `norm_ratio` (plus a couple of bookkeeping columns `summarize_dimensionality()` doesn't need). A small stand-in with the same shape, in place of `read.csv("dimensionality_results.csv")`:

```{r summarize-dim-example}
set.seed(2)
n_restarts <- 5
# A loss that drops sharply through d = 2, then plateaus -- the same
# shape as the worked example in vignette("embedding_vignette").
true_loss_by_d <- c(`1` = 0.60, `2` = 0.51, `3` = 0.447, `4` = 0.447, `5` = 0.447)

dimensionality_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:5, function(d) {
  data.frame(
    d          = d,
    restart    = seq_len(n_restarts),
    loss       = true_loss_by_d[[as.character(d)]] + rnorm(n_restarts, sd = 0.006),
    accuracy   = 0.75 + 0.01 * d + rnorm(n_restarts, sd = 0.01),
    epoch      = sample(2000:5000, n_restarts),
    norm_ratio = 1 + abs(rnorm(n_restarts, sd = 0.05))
  )
}))

summarize_dimensionality(dimensionality_results, n_restarts = n_restarts)
```

`n_restarts` must be passed explicitly here (unlike `estimate_dimensionality()`, which already knows it) since it's needed for the standard-error term behind `best_d`'s one-SE rule -- see `?estimate_dimensionality`'s "How `best_d` is determined" for what that rule is actually doing. It's assumed constant across every `d`, matching every Condor workflow's own one-restart-count-for-the-whole-stage design.

`learning_curve_results.csv` follows the same idea, one row per `(fraction, restart)`:

```{r summarize-learning-curve-example}
fractions <- c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0)

learning_curve_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fractions, function(f) {
  data.frame(
    fraction   = f,
    n_train    = round(f * 1000),
    restart    = seq_len(n_restarts),
    loss       = 0.60 - 0.10 * f + rnorm(n_restarts, sd = 0.008),
    accuracy   = 0.65 + 0.10 * f + rnorm(n_restarts, sd = 0.01),
    epoch      = sample(2000:5000, n_restarts),
    norm_ratio = 1 + abs(rnorm(n_restarts, sd = 0.05))
  )
}))

summarize_learning_curve(learning_curve_results)
```

A rising `mean_accuracy`/falling `mean_loss` that's still climbing steeply at `fraction = 1.0` is the signal to collect more data before trusting the final embedding; one that's already flattened out by `fraction = 0.75` or so means the fit has enough triplets and more participants would mostly buy diminishing returns — see `?estimate_learning_curve` for the full interpretation.

---

## Workflow 2: Group-difference permutation test

`condor_group_diff_workflow.py` tests whether two participant groups' embeddings differ reliably: it fits a separate embedding for each true group, measures their Procrustes correlation, and compares that to a null distribution built from many random re-partitions of the pooled participants — **matched to the true groups' sizes**, not a blanket 50/50 split, since embedding quality depends on how much data went into a fit. See `?group_difference_test` for the full statistical rationale (this workflow is its large-scale Condor companion, same logic, independent implementation).

**This workflow needs two R scripts** (`condor_group_fit.R` and `condor_group_compare.R`), not one — easy to under-count by analogy to Workflow 1's single `condor_fit.R`. Both must be present alongside `condor_group_diff_workflow.py`, which is already guaranteed if you sparse-cloned `inst/condor/` as a whole.

**Inputs:** raw triplet-judgment data, not precomputed embeddings — fitting every embedding is the whole point of the permutation test.

1. A combined triplet-judgment CSV (see the general procedure above).
2. A group-labels CSV, exactly two columns:

   ```csv
   worker_id,group
   p001,patient
   p002,patient
   ...
   p050,control
   ```

   Must cover *exactly* the same worker IDs as the triplet CSV (checked, with a clear error listing any mismatches), with exactly two distinct `group` values, each with at least 3 participants.

**Choose `d` beforehand** — fixed across the true split and every null permutation, never re-selected per replicate, since that would be both prohibitively slow (hundreds of permutations × a full dimensionality search each) and would entangle dimensionality selection with the group-difference test itself.

```{r run-group-diff, engine = "bash"}
python3 condor_group_diff_workflow.py triplet_data.csv group_labels.csv my_params.yml
```

This runs in two Condor stages — Stage 1 fits one embedding per (replicate, side) pair (the true split contributes 2, each of `n_permutations` null replicates contributes 2 more), waits for all of them, then Stage 2 computes one Procrustes comparison per replicate — followed by local aggregation. Outputs in `output_dir`:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `stage1_fit/embedding_repN_side{A,B}.csv` | Every fitted embedding (true split = replicate 0) |
| `stage2_compare/compare_N.csv` | Each replicate's Procrustes correlation |
| `null_distribution.csv` | All `1 + n_permutations` correlations, with an `is_true` flag |
| `summary.csv` | `observed_correlation`, `p_value`, and null-distribution mean/SD |
| `run_manifest.txt` | Group sizes, `d`, `n_permutations`, the final result, container image, for provenance |

---

## Workflow 3: Per-participant individual embeddings

`condor_individual_embeddings_workflow.py` fits a **separate** embedding for each unique `worker_id` in a triplet dataset — one Condor job per participant — then concatenates every result into a single CSV indexed by `worker_id` and `item`. This is the large-scale companion to `run_embeddings_from_list()`'s per-individual output, for when fitting every participant locally (even multicore, via `future`/`future.apply`) would take too long.

**Only one input file is needed** — a combined triplet-judgment CSV (see the general procedure above); every distinct `worker_id` found in it gets its own fit. Unlike Workflow 2, no separate labels file is required.

```{r run-individual, engine = "bash"}
python3 condor_individual_embeddings_workflow.py triplet_data.csv my_params.yml
```

This is a single Condor stage (one job per participant) plus a local, non-Condor concatenation step — there's no comparison stage, unlike Workflow 2, since there's nothing to compare across participants here. Outputs in `output_dir`:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `stage1_fit/embedding_workerN.csv` | Each participant's own fitted embedding (`worker_id`, `item`, `dim_0`, `dim_1`, …) |
| `embeddings.csv` | Every participant's embedding concatenated, indexed by `worker_id` and `item` |
| `run_manifest.txt` | Participant count, `d`, container image, for provenance |

**Choose `d` generously, not exactly.** Unlike the other two workflows, `d` here does not need to be each participant's own "correct" dimensionality — different participants may genuinely have different latent dimensionality, and re-running a full per-participant dimensionality search on Condor would be expensive to repeat hundreds of times. Instead, fit everyone at one shared, generously high `d` (with headroom above what you'd expect any single participant to need), then reduce each participant's own embedding back down locally after pulling `embeddings.csv` down from the cluster:

```{r reduce-after-pull}
library(tripletTools)

individual <- get.combined("embeddings.csv", eflag = TRUE)   # split back out per worker_id
triplets   <- get.combined("triplet_data.csv")               # same, for the original judgments

result <- reduce_embedding_dimension(
  embedding    = individual[["p001"]],
  triplet_data = triplets[["p001"]],
  variance_threshold = 0.95
)

result$k                # this participant's reduced dimensionality
result$accuracy_full    # accuracy at the original, generous d
result$accuracy         # accuracy at the reduced k -- should be close to accuracy_full
```

`reduce_embedding_dimension()` reduces via PCA on each participant's own fitted coordinates (not classical MDS — the two give identical results when you already have exact Euclidean coordinates in hand, so MDS would just be a more expensive detour to the same answer) and reports triplet-prediction accuracy under the reduced embedding evaluated against *every* triplet that participant judged, not a held-out subset — deliberately, so the chosen dimensionality isn't sensitive to which triplets happened to land in that participant's own random train/test split. See `?reduce_embedding_dimension` for the full rationale and its `diagnostics` output for inspecting the whole variance/accuracy curve rather than trusting a single threshold blindly.

---

## Workflow 4: Joint geometry+choice-model manifold estimation

`condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py` jointly estimates, for every participant, a position on a shared 1-D latent geometry manifold (a real re-fit embedding at that position) **and** their own choice-model shape parameter alpha — rather than assuming, as every other workflow in this package does, that everyone shares one fixed choice model (the crowd-kernel default) and only their geometry differs. Geometry and alpha are estimated **independently** of each other, not tied to a single shared curve — see *Does alpha need to be tied to geometry?* below for why.

### Why this workflow exists

Whether this is worth the extra machinery is an empirical question, not an assumption, and it was tested before any of this was built. The real, already-in-production baseline is: fit each participant their own individual embedding, score it with the standard shared choice model. On real Gabor-triplet data (orientation + contrast, participants instructed to judge orientation only — a dataset with documented, qualitative individual differences in which stimulus dimension people actually attend to), a leave-one-out comparison found that jointly re-fitting each participant's embedding under their own current alpha, alternating with re-estimating the shared population curve, beat that baseline decisively on held-out validation-trial log-likelihood (20 of 24 participants, paired $t=3.74$, $p=0.0011$), with a weaker but same-direction trend in raw accuracy — exactly the asymmetry expected when the gain comes from calibration (getting each person's own alpha right) rather than from flipping which option gets predicted, since accuracy is structurally insensitive to alpha for this choice-model family. The same comparison, run on a dataset without that kind of qualitative mismatch, showed no advantage at all — this is not a workflow worth reaching for by default, only when individual differences look like genuinely different people attending to genuinely different things, not just noisier versions of the same thing. The full write-up, including why those two datasets give different answers, lives outside this package in the lab's own research documentation, not here.

Full-scale production runs (24 then 30 participants on the orientation+contrast dataset) confirmed this holds up outside the small leave-one-out pilot, and sharpened it further: an in-sample comparison alone can't distinguish "real cross-participant structure" from two more mundane explanations (self-contribution, and recalibrating the choice-model noise parameter rather than the geometry) — see *Summarizing and interpreting a run* below for the diagnostic this project now runs to tell them apart, and why it matters before trusting any single comparison number.

### Does alpha need to be tied to geometry?

The original design (and the LOO test above) tied alpha to the same position driving geometry: `alpha(t) = exp(beta0 + beta1*t)`, one smooth curve fit jointly across everyone. That coupling was never load-bearing, and later testing removed it. A controlled decomposition -- own vs. pooled embedding, crossed with alpha fixed at 1 vs. the fitted curve -- found the production run's advantage over baseline separates into two pieces, not one: embedding-pooling alone (alpha held fixed) already recovered most of the combined effect, leaving only one open question -- does the curve's own position-dependence add anything a plain, independently-estimated per-person alpha (properly regularized toward the population) would not? Tested directly on both validated datasets, the answer was no: a per-person alpha, estimated by its own bounded-grid profiled MLE and shrunk toward a precision-weighted population mean (a standard random-effects, DerSimonian-Laird empirical-Bayes estimator -- which also turned out to matter: a naive unweighted shrinkage estimate collapsed to zero between-person variance on both datasets, traced to a few poorly-identified individuals distorting it as much as well-identified ones), tied with the coupled curve on the dataset where coupling helped at all, and avoided a real liability on the other dataset, where geometry carries no individual-differences signal and tying alpha to it has nothing to gain and real noise to inherit. This decoupled design is now the only one implemented -- the full comparison, including why a plain population mean among the per-person estimates themselves needed the same precision-weighting to avoid being dominated by a couple of runaway individual fits (one unconstrained per-person optimizer diverged past $10^{10}$ for a participant whose own data was highly self-consistent), lives in `triplet_choice_and_loss.Rmd` outside this package.

### Unlike Workflow 1-3's simplicity, this one is iterative

The other three workflows here are one- or two-stage: submit a batch, wait, optionally submit a second batch, aggregate locally. This workflow alternates for `n_outer` iterations, each needing its own submit-and-wait round:

(a) **[Condor, parallel]** refit every participant's own embedding under their current alpha (their own independently-estimated, shrinkage-regularized value -- not a function of position), warm-started from their previous embedding (their original individual fit on iteration 1) — one Condor batch per iteration, covering every participant's refit at once, not one batch per participant per iteration (submitting that granularly would pay Condor's queueing/startup latency far more times than necessary).

(b) **[Condor, single job]** re-align the newly-refit embeddings, refine each participant's position via a profiled choice-model-likelihood search (scored at their own current, fixed alpha -- not a curve evaluated at the candidate position), and re-estimate each participant's own alpha (bounded-grid profiled MLE, then empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward the population). This step is cheap (seconds) but still runs inside the container as its own single-job Condor batch, not as a local Rscript call on the submit node — an earlier version of this workflow ran it locally, on the reasoning that another Condor round-trip wasn't worth it for something this cheap, but a real submit node turned out to have no R installation and no clear way to add one. Moving this step into Condor too restored the "no R needed on the submit node" property every workflow in this vignette is supposed to have.

### Resuming an interrupted or extended run

`n_outer` is a total-iteration *target*, not a fixed count: rerunning the same command against the same `output_dir` resumes after the last iteration with all expected outputs present (`positions.csv` and `alpha.csv`), rather than starting over. This is how a run gets extended after the fact (a real production run's per-participant position trajectories took considerably longer to settle than first expected, with a specific subgroup still correcting from an early overshoot at iteration 8 — raising `n_outer` and rerunning let that finish without discarding the compute already spent) — just edit `n_outer` upward in `my_params.yml` and rerun the same command. A `--fresh` flag forces starting over regardless. Resuming checks that the triplet/embeddings inputs match the original run's recorded `setup/worker_ids.txt`/`item_order.txt` exactly, and refuses (with a clear error, not a silent mismatch) rather than risk misattributing a `person{i}.csv`-indexed position or embedding to the wrong participant.

### Inputs and deployment

**Two** files are needed, not one: a combined triplet-judgment CSV, and a combined individual-embeddings CSV (e.g. from Workflow 3) giving every participant's own starting embedding — this workflow refits from an existing fit, it doesn't produce one from scratch.

```{r run-joint-manifold, engine = "bash"}
python3 condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py triplet_data.csv embeddings.csv my_params.yml
```

Outputs in `output_dir`:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `setup/` | Per-participant original embeddings and pre-indexed train/test/pooled triplet files, plus `worker_ids.txt`/`item_order.txt` (the canonical order every other file in the run shares, and what resuming checks against) — built once, reused every iteration |
| `iterN/refit/embeddings/personI.csv` | Participant I's refit embedding after outer iteration N |
| `iterN/aligned/personI.csv` | That iteration's GPA-aligned embeddings — needs the update step's `transfer_output_files` to include `aligned` explicitly (HTCondor's default output transfer picks up new plain files but not new subdirectories on its own); missing on a run from before that was fixed |
| `iterN/positions.csv` | That iteration's updated manifold positions |
| `iterN/alpha.csv` | Each participant's own re-estimated alpha (shrinkage-regularized), plus diagnostics (`log_alpha_raw`/`se_log_alpha` -- the unregularized per-person MLE and its precision, `shrinkage_weight`, `tau2`/`pop_mean_alpha` -- population-level, same on every row, and geometry `bandwidth`, unrelated to alpha) |
| `final_embeddings.csv`, `final_positions.csv` | Every participant's final refit embedding and manifold position. **Not the artifact to evaluate or predict with** — a real production run showed this specific output degrading with more outer iterations in a way that looks exactly like textbook overfitting, which turned out to be a measurement artifact: the leave-one-out validation above never evaluated a held-out participant's own refit embedding at all, only the kernel-smoothed pooled estimate below. Use that instead. |
| `final_alpha.csv` | Every participant's final alpha — already the shrinkage-regularized value, no further computation needed |
| `final_smoothed_embeddings.csv` | **The validated geometry estimator.** The kernel-smoothed pooled embedding at each participant's own position — this is what the decisive comparison above actually evaluated (paired with `final_alpha.csv`). Requires the final iteration's `aligned/` output; skipped with a printed note (not a failure) if that's missing. |
| `final_grand_mean_embedding.csv` | A plain, *position-independent* average across every participant's aligned embedding — the same embedding for everyone, no kernel weighting. Comparing this to `final_smoothed_embeddings.csv` is how to tell whether a participant's own recovered position is doing anything real, or whether pooling alone (noise reduction, no manifold needed) explains the whole benefit — see *Summarizing and interpreting a run* below. |
| `run_manifest.txt` | Participant count, `d`, `n_outer`, final mean alpha, container image, for provenance |

### Summarizing and interpreting a run

`summarize_joint_estimation()` (R package, not a Condor file) reads `output_dir` directly and writes a self-contained Markdown report, so the diagnostics below don't have to be redone by hand for every new dataset run through this workflow:

```{r summarize-joint-manifold}
library(tripletTools)

# Convergence diagnostics (position AND alpha trajectory flagging --
# estimated independently now, each gets its own check -- an
# embedding-geometry grid) need nothing beyond the output directory itself:
res <- summarize_joint_estimation("condor_joint_manifold_output")

# The held-out validation comparison and `loo_trajectory_accuracy()` check
# need the *original* combined triplet data too, since validation trials
# are deliberately never passed to this workflow at all
# (assign_sample_sets()'s "holdout" convention) -- they can't be recovered
# from output_dir alone, unlike the original baseline embeddings, which
# already live under setup/original_embeddings/ and need no extra argument.
res <- summarize_joint_estimation(
  "condor_joint_manifold_output",
  triplet_data = read.csv("triplet_data.csv")
)
res$decomposition
```

The report's comparison table is deliberately not just "does the production estimate beat the baseline" — that single comparison conflates two different things (pooling across participants, and recalibrating the choice-model noise parameter), either of which alone could produce a win with no real geometric structure behind it. The decisive row is `(c) position-weighted pool vs. (e) grand mean`: if a participant's own recovered position adds nothing on top of a plain, position-independent average of everyone, there is no evidence of real manifold structure, only ordinary noise reduction from pooling. Run live on two real datasets, this told two genuinely different stories: on one (orientation-only Gabors, no documented individual-difference axis), the grand mean alone recovered the *entire* pooling benefit (position added nothing more, $p=0.53$) and even reached a Procrustes correlation of 0.988 with the known true geometry — individual embeddings there are best understood as noisy estimates of one shared representation, not evidence of a real manifold. On the other (orientation+contrast, the dataset *Why this workflow exists* above is based on), the grand mean did *not* reliably beat the baseline on its own, while position-weighting on top of it was itself a significant, additional improvement ($p=0.0080$) — exactly the asymmetry that justifies this workflow's extra machinery for that dataset and not the other one. Neither conclusion was assumed going in; both came from running the same report on real data.

### `mode: loo` — deliberately not the default next step

**Only `mode: fit` is implemented** — one joint estimate across every participant, no held-out evaluation. `mode: loo` (the full leave-one-out validation used for the decisive comparison above, re-running the entire alternating procedure once per held-out participant) is not a planned near-term follow-up so much as a deliberately deprioritized one: it is expensive (one full production run per participant) and mainly answers a *magnitude* question — how much does the actual deployed estimator help a genuinely new participant, quantitatively. The two cheap checks in *Summarizing and interpreting a run* above (the grand-mean decomposition and `loo_trajectory_accuracy()`, neither needing a Condor run) already answer the *existence* question — is there real structure at all — convincingly and for near-zero cost, and are the recommended first step on any new dataset. Build `mode: loo` only when the magnitude specifically needs to be trustworthy on its own, e.g. a headline effect size for publication.
